issues.legal_issue: A right acquired from a proprietor to collect forest produce after proprietary interests in the land pass to the state is a proprietary right that passes to the state.
material_facts: The claimant acquired rights from land proprietors to collect forest produce for years after the proprietary interests in the forests were to vest in the state.
The state took charge of the forests and prevented the claimant from exercising the acquired rights.
issues.conclusion: The right to collect forest produce was a proprietary right and vested in the state under section 4(1)(a) of the Abolition Act; the acquired rights did not fall within the exceptions in section 5.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1)(a) provides for proprietary rights, including rights in forests, to vest in the state free of encumbrances. State of Madhya Pradesh v. Yakinuddin held that rights to propagate lac and collect forest produce acquired from proprietors were proprietary rights within that provision; it expressly overruled the contrary view in Chhotabhai Jethabhai Patel & Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh. The court held that the present case was governed by Yakinuddin.

predicates.forest_produce_rights_case: The dispute concerns rights to collect forest produce from land whose proprietary interests pass to the state.
predicates.rights_acquired_from_proprietor: A person acquired the forest produce rights from the land proprietor.
predicates.exercise_due_after_state_vesting: The acquired rights were to be exercised after the proprietary interests in the land passed to the state.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns forest produce rights acquired from a proprietor for exercise after the land's proprietary interests pass to the state, those rights vest in the state.

issues.legal_issue: A contract with the government that does not comply with mandatory constitutional execution formalities is void and cannot be validated by estoppel or ratification.
material_facts: The claimant paid a deposit after an official accepted the bid for rights to collect lac from the forests.
The claimant collected some lac under the arrangement.
The parties did not dispute that the formal requirements for government contracts in Article 299(1) had not been complied with.
issues.conclusion: The contract was void because it did not comply with Article 299(1), and neither estoppel nor ratification could validate it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 299(1) of the Constitution, like section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, imposes mandatory formal requirements for government contracts. Those requirements protect the government and the public from unauthorised contracts, so they cannot be waived or dispensed with. The court relied on Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India and State of West Bengal v. B. K. Mondal & Sons.

predicates.government_contract_dispute: The case concerns whether an agreement made with the government is legally effective.
predicates.agreement_made_with_government: A person entered an agreement with the government through an official acting for it.
predicates.mandatory_execution_formalities_absent: The agreement did not satisfy the mandatory formal requirements for government contracts.

issues.definition: If an agreement with the government fails mandatory execution formalities, it is void and cannot be made valid by estoppel or ratification.

issues.legal_issue: A person seeking restitution for a benefit conferred under a void contract must account for benefits received in the transaction, and restitution may be denied when reliable accounting evidence is not produced.
material_facts: The claimant sought return of a deposit paid under the void arrangement.
The claimant collected lac under the arrangement but did not provide reliable evidence of the extent of the work done or the profits made.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to restitution or a refund because he failed to provide sufficient reliable evidence to account for what he had received from the transaction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act permits compensation or restoration when a person lawfully does something for another or delivers something to another, does not intend to act gratuitously, and the other person enjoys the benefit. This is a restitutionary or quasi-contractual obligation, not enforcement of the void contract or recovery of damages for its breach. A person seeking restitution must account for what that person received in the transaction. The court applied Fibrosa v. Fairbairn and Nelson v. Larholt.

predicates.restitution_claim_under_void_government_: A person seeks restitution for a transaction arising from a void agreement with the government.
predicates.claimant_received_transaction_benefit: The claimant received a benefit from the transaction for which restitution is sought.
predicates.claimant_failed_reliable_accounting: The claimant did not provide reliable evidence accounting for the benefits received from the transaction.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeking restitution under a void government agreement received a transaction benefit but failed to account for it reliably, restitution is denied.
